claims.note: The evidence consists only of navigation/menu content from the NASA page. The headline confirms Crew-13 docking occurred but provides no details about the time (under 8 hours) or method (orbital phasing). The actual article text that would contain these specifics is not present in the evidence.

The Wikipedia article on space rendezvous explicitly states: 'If the target is ahead in the orbit and the tracking vehicle increases speed, its altitude also increases, actually moving it away from the target.' It further explains that 'The higher altitude then increases orbital period due to Kepler's third law.' This directly supports the claim that forward thrust raises orbit altitude rather than directly increasing speed relative to the target.

The Wikipedia article on orbit phasing explains: 'If spacecraft is behind the final position on the same orbit, the spacecraft must slow down to enter a smaller, faster phasing orbit to catch up to final position.' This describes a spacecraft in a lower orbit being overtaken by or catching up to a target, matching the claim's description of orbital phasing.

learner.main_idea: Catching the space station is about getting into the right higher orbit ahead of it and letting the station catch up, not about speeding up to chase it.
how_it_works_steps: Think of a roundabout: the inner lane (lower orbit) travels a shorter distance per lap and moves faster; the outer lane (higher orbit) travels a longer distance per lap and moves slower.
Apply forward thrust to raise the spacecraft to a higher orbit (outer lane).
In that higher orbit the spacecraft moves slower and can position itself ahead of the station.
The station, staying in a lower, faster orbit, will lap the Earth more quickly and eventually catch up to the spacecraft.
When both are in the same orbit they meet, allowing docking.

viewer_would_call_fake.why: The capsule approaching the station 'from below' violates orbital mechanics - a spacecraft that raised its orbit to get ahead would be ABOVE the station (farther from Earth), not below it. Space-savvy viewers would recognize this as physically impossible.

Self-contradicting camera instructions ('static shot' vs 'push in') suggest production confusion, and the resulting visual of the capsule drifting downward toward the station looks like chasing from below, which contradicts the stated mechanism of 'station catches up from behind.'
